DOCUMENT:
Feasibility Study: Weekly Separate Food Waste Collection
Waste and Environmental Services, Thornbury District Council, October 2026

1. Purpose
Councils in England are required to introduce weekly separate food waste collections for households. This study assesses how Thornbury can deliver the service district-wide from April 2027, based on a six-month pilot, and estimates its costs and savings.

2. The pilot
From January to June 2026, 4,000 households in three wards received a 23-litre outdoor caddy, a 5-litre kitchen caddy and a supply of compostable liners, with collection every week on the same day as their existing bin collection. The pilot wards were chosen to include a mix of houses and flats, and of urban and village streets.

Table 1. Pilot participation by housing type (average weekly set-out, Jan-Jun 2026)
Housing type | Households | Participating households | Participation rate | Food waste per participating household per week
Houses | 3,200 | 2,112 | 66% | 1.9 kg
Flats | 800 | 168 | 21% | 1.4 kg
All | 4,000 | 2,280 | 57% | 1.9 kg

Participation was broadly similar across housing types, which gives us confidence that the service can be rolled out uniformly across the district without a separate approach for flats. Residents' feedback was positive, with 81% of surveyed pilot households rating the service good or very good. Contamination with packaging and other non-food items was low, at under 2% by weight in spot checks carried out at the treatment plant, and missed-collection reports fell steadily after the first month.

3. District-wide projection
Thornbury has 52,000 households, of which about 20% are flats. Applying the pilot's 64% participation rate and 1.9 kg per participating household per week across the district gives about 3,290 tonnes of food waste a year.

4. Treatment
Collected food waste would be taken to Brookfield anaerobic digestion (AD) plant, 14 miles from our depot, at a gate fee of £38 per tonne. Food waste that stays in the residual bin is incinerated at a cost of £112 per tonne. Every tonne diverted therefore saves £74, or around £243,000 a year on the projected tonnage. Brookfield has confirmed that it can offer the Council up to 1,800 tonnes a year of contracted capacity until its planned expansion is completed in 2029. The next nearest AD plant is 46 miles away.

5. Costs
Table 2. Annual cost of district-wide service
Item | Annual cost
Vehicles: six food waste vehicles at £165,000 each, depreciated over seven years | £141,400
Crews: six crews of two at £34,000 per operative | £408,000
Fuel and maintenance | £96,000
Caddies, liners and communications (annualised) | £88,000
Total | £733,400

Against the disposal saving of £243,000, the net annual cost is about £490,000. The Government has indicated that new-burdens funding will be provided for the service; our provisional allocation is £520,000 a year, which would cover the net cost in full.

6. Implementation
Vehicles must be ordered by December 2026 for delivery in March 2027. Caddies would be delivered to all households in March 2027, with a leaflet and a three-month supply of liners. Collections would start in the week of 5 April 2027. Crews will be recruited from February 2027 and trained on the new vehicles during March. A dedicated phone line and web page will handle caddy requests and missed collections during the first three months of the service.

7. Recommendation
The pilot demonstrates strong participation and resident satisfaction, and the service can be delivered on a uniform basis across the district. With treatment at Brookfield and new-burdens funding, the service is fully funded. We recommend that Cabinet approve the district-wide roll-out from April 2027 and authorise the vehicle order.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [inconsistency] at: "Applying the pilot's 64% participation rate" -- Table 1 gives the pilot participation rate as 57% overall (66% houses, 21% flats); the projection applies a '64%' pilot participation rate. (64% x 52,000 x 1.9 kg x 52 = about 3,290 t; at 57% it would be about 2,930 t.)
2. [misread_evidence] at: "Participation was broadly similar across housing types" -- Table 1 shows participation of 66% in houses but only 21% in flats, a very large difference. The claim misreads the table, and the conclusion that a uniform service needs no separate approach for flats rests on it.
3. [missing_consideration] at: "Every tonne diverted therefore saves £74, or around £243,000 a year on the projected tonnage." -- The saving assumes all projected tonnage (about 3,290 t) goes to Brookfield at £38/t, but the document states Brookfield can take only 1,800 t a year until 2029 and the next plant is 46 miles away. The excess tonnage's treatment and haulage cost is never addressed, though the 'fully funded' conclusion depends on it.

REVIEW:
# Review: Feasibility Study for Weekly Separate Food Waste Collection

**Verdict:** The arithmetic in the cost table is correct, but three errors in the inputs reverse the study's two main conclusions:
1. The pilot shows flats participating at a third of the rate of houses, not "broadly similar."
2. The tonnage projection uses a participation rate (64%) that appears nowhere in the pilot data.
3. Brookfield can take only 1,800 tonnes a year, but the savings assume it takes all of it.

Corrected for these, the service is probably **not** fully funded by the £520,000 allocation, and flats need their own approach.

## What checks out

- **Table 1 rates are correct:** 2,112/3,200 = 66%; 168/800 = 21%; 2,280/4,000 = 57%.
- **Table 2 is correct:** vehicles £990,000 ÷ 7 = £141,400; crews 12 × £34,000 = £408,000; total £733,400.
- **The saving per tonne is correct:** £112 − £38 = £74 a tonne. On the study's 3,290 tonnes that gives £243,000, and the net cost of £490,400 follows.

## 1. Flats participation is not "broadly similar"

Table 1 shows houses at **66%** and flats at **21%**. That is less than a third of the rate, and flats that do take part also put out less (1.4 kg against 1.9 kg).

The pilot is evidence *for* a separate approach to flats, not against one. Typical measures are communal bins, bin-store changes and work with landlords and managing agents. Thornbury has about 10,400 flats, and the duty to provide the service covers them too. A uniform rollout would leave most of them not taking part. A flats plan should be costed, and it isn't in Table 2.

## 2. The tonnage projection uses the wrong participation rate

Section 3 applies "the pilot's 64% participation rate," but the pilot's overall rate was **57%**, and 64% doesn't appear anywhere.

The district's housing mix (20% flats) is the same as the pilot's, so projecting by housing type gives:
- Houses: 41,600 × 66% × 1.9 kg × 52 ≈ 2,713 t
- Flats: 10,400 × 21% × 1.4 kg × 52 ≈ 159 t
- **Total ≈ 2,870 tonnes a year, not 3,290** (about 13% lower)

Even this may be optimistic:
- The pilot ran for only six months, and participation often declines after the first months of a new service.
- Pilot households had a supply of liners, but the rollout includes only three months' worth. If liners stop after that, participation may fall.

## 3. Brookfield can't take the projected tonnage

Section 4 says Brookfield's contracted capacity is **up to 1,800 tonnes a year until 2029**. Even the corrected projection of 2,870 tonnes exceeds that by about 1,070 tonnes, and the study's own 3,290 exceeds it by about 1,490.

The extra tonnage would have to go to the next plant, 46 miles away. Its gate fee is unknown, and the extra haulage costs are not in the budget. So:
- The £74 saving per tonne is guaranteed only on 1,800 tonnes, which is **£133,200**, not £243,000.
- "Treatment is local" holds for only part of the tonnage.

## 4. Effect on funding

With the £74 saving on 1,800 tonnes and, conservatively, no saving on the remainder:

| | Study | Corrected |
|---|---|---|
| Annual cost | £733,400 | £733,400 + haulage to the 46-mile plant |
| Disposal saving | £243,000 | ~£133,200 (+/− whatever the remaining tonnage saves or costs) |
| Net cost | £490,400 | ~£600,000+ |
| Provisional allocation | £520,000 | £520,000 |
| Gap | +£30,000 surplus | ~£80,000 shortfall or more |

The outcome for the remaining tonnage could fall either way. It might still save money if the second plant's gate fee plus haulage comes in under £112 a tonne, or cost more if it doesn't. **What would settle it:** a gate fee quote from the 46-mile plant and a haulage estimate.

Two further funding points:
- The allocation is described as **provisional**.
- Check whether the incineration contract has a minimum-tonnage clause. If it does, diverting waste may not save the full £112 a tonne.

## 5. Costs not shown

The author describes every cost line as shown. These appear to be missing:
- Haulage to the second plant (see §3).
- A flats approach: communal containers, bin-store works (§1).
- Ongoing liners, if they will be supplied beyond the first three months.
- Relief staff for holidays and sickness, and a spare vehicle. Six vehicles and six crews leaves no cover.
- Supervision and management. Clarify whether the £34,000 per operative includes employer's National Insurance and pension costs.

## 6. Timetable and statutory deadline

- **Vehicle lead time.** Ordering in December for March delivery assumes a three-month lead time. Many councils are buying these vehicles at the same time. Get a written lead time from the supplier before relying on it.
- **Recruitment.** Starting crew recruitment in February leaves about a month to fill twelve posts before training in March.
- **Statutory deadline.** My understanding is that, under the Simpler Recycling rules, English councils were due to begin weekly household food waste collections by 31 March 2026, with later dates possible under transitional arrangements. If that's right, an April 2027 start needs either confirmation that Thornbury qualifies for a later date or a statement that the council is currently non-compliant. Please check this against current Defra guidance rather than relying on my summary.

## 7. Smaller points

- **Response rate unknown.** The 81% satisfaction figure doesn't say how many households responded. Participating households are more likely to answer.
- **Unrepresentative period.** Six months, January to June, may not reflect a full year of food waste volumes.

## Summary of the author's claims

| Claim | Assessment |
|---|---|
| Projections based on how residents actually behave | They use a 64% rate the pilot doesn't show; the pilot gives 57% |
| Participation held up across houses and flats | Wrong: 66% vs 21% |
| A single uniform service will work | Not supported; flats need a separate approach |
| Every cost line shown | Missing: excess-tonnage haulage, flats, relief staff, spare vehicle, ongoing liners |
| Net cost ~£490,000, fully covered | Likely ~£600,000 or more; probably not covered, pending the second plant's costs |
| Treatment is local | Only for 1,800 tonnes; the rest goes 46 miles |
| Timetable works back from vehicle lead time | Plausible but unconfirmed; recruitment is tight |
| Evidence-based and fully funded | The pilot evidence contradicts two key conclusions; funding is uncertain |

## Suggested revisions before this goes to Cabinet

1. Project tonnage by housing type using the pilot rates (about 2,870 t), with a lower scenario that allows for participation declining over time.
2. Get a gate fee from the 46-mile plant, cost the haulage, and rerun the net cost.
3. Design and cost a flats-specific service.
4. Add the missing cost lines and confirm the employment on-costs.
5. Confirm the statutory start date and whether a transitional arrangement applies.
6. Present funding as a range against the provisional allocation, not as "fully funded."

The recommendation to order vehicles by December may still be right, given the lead time. But Cabinet should approve it knowing the funding gap is open, not on the basis that the service is fully funded.
